args.task_description: Evaluate whether GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol use disorder symptoms, and map likely neurobiological mechanisms.

attribution: requester: R. H. Chen (Northbridge Medical Group)

hypotheses.content: GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment produces a clinically meaningful reduction in alcohol consumption (e.g., drinks/week and heavy drinking days) versus placebo/usual care in adults with alcohol use disorder over ≥12 weeks.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Falsified if, across adequately powered RCTs (or meta-analysis thereof), the pooled effect on pre-specified consumption outcomes is null or favors control (e.g., SMD ~0 with 95% CI excluding clinically meaningful benefit), or if any apparent benefit disappears after accounting for differential dropout and concomitant AUD pharmacotherapy.

plan.description: Identify RCTs/controlled studies of semaglutide, liraglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide (and related GLP-1RAs) in AUD or heavy drinkers; extract standardized alcohol outcomes, follow-up duration, and dropout; assess risk of bias and run random-effects meta-analysis where possible.
plan.timeline: 1–2 days for search/screening; 2–3 days for extraction/ROB; 1 day for synthesis

hypotheses.content: Any observed reduction in alcohol use with GLP-1RAs is mediated primarily by changes in craving/reward valuation rather than by nonspecific effects of weight loss, nausea, or reduced caloric intake.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Falsified if alcohol reductions remain fully explained by proxies of adverse effects/energy intake (e.g., nausea severity, caloric reduction, weight change) with no independent association between GLP-1RA exposure and validated craving scales, or if mechanistic endpoints (craving, cue-reactivity) show no change despite reduced drinking.

plan.description: Extract mediator variables (weight change, nausea, appetite, craving scales, cue-reactivity tasks) from trials/observational studies; test mediation/adjustment logic qualitatively and, where data allow, quantitatively using reported adjusted models or individual participant data requests.

hypotheses.content: GLP-1RA efficacy for reducing alcohol use disorder symptoms is more likely to be detectable in subgroups with obesity/insulin resistance (or metabolic syndrome) than in metabolically healthy individuals with AUD.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Falsified if subgroup analyses (pre-specified or credible post hoc) show no interaction by BMI/metabolic markers, or if effects are similar (within statistical uncertainty) across metabolic strata in multiple independent datasets.

plan.description: Catalog trials/observational cohorts reporting baseline BMI, HbA1c, insulin resistance proxies, and alcohol outcomes; extract interaction estimates or stratified results; evaluate credibility of subgroup findings using ICEMAN-style criteria and triangulate with preclinical evidence.

args.task_description: Evaluate whether GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol use disorder symptoms, and map likely neurobiological mechanisms.

attribution: Requester: R. H. Chen (Northbridge Medical Group)

hypotheses.content: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol craving and consumption by decreasing dopaminergic reward signaling in mesolimbic circuitry (VTA→nucleus accumbens), reducing cue-reactivity.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: In randomized or well-controlled studies, GLP-1RA treatment does NOT reduce validated cue-reactivity measures (e.g., fMRI ventral striatum response to alcohol cues) nor alter dopamine-related biomarkers compared with placebo, despite adequate exposure and adherence.

plan.description: Search human and animal studies linking GLP-1RA to alcohol intake, cue-reactivity, and mesolimbic dopamine measures; prioritize RCTs and mechanistic neuroimaging; extract effect sizes and endpoints.

attribution: Requester: R. H. Chen (Northbridge Medical Group)

hypotheses.content: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol intake by modulating stress/anxiety pathways (HPA axis activity and amygdala reactivity), thereby lowering stress-induced relapse.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Across controlled studies, GLP-1RA treatment does NOT change stress-induced drinking outcomes, cortisol/HPA markers, or amygdala reactivity compared with placebo, when baseline stress/anxiety is elevated and relapse paradigms are properly implemented.

plan.description: Identify studies measuring stress-induced alcohol intake or relapse with GLP-1RA exposure; extract outcomes for cortisol/HPA markers and anxiety-related behavioral endpoints.
resources_needed: Human experimental stress paradigms in AUD

attribution: Requester: R. H. Chen (Northbridge Medical Group)

hypotheses.content: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol use via metabolic/visceral feedback (improved glycemic stability and reduced postprandial reward drive), indirectly decreasing alcohol-seeking behavior particularly in individuals with insulin resistance.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: No differential reduction in alcohol consumption is observed in insulin-resistant vs insulin-sensitive subgroups, and changes in glycemic variability or insulin resistance markers do not correlate with changes in alcohol outcomes in controlled analyses.

plan.description: Collect RCT/observational datasets where GLP-1RA exposure and metabolic markers (HbA1c, fasting insulin, CGM variability) are available alongside alcohol outcomes; test mediation/moderation by insulin resistance.

attribution: Requester: R. H. Chen (Northbridge Medical Group)

hypotheses.content: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol consumption through nausea/conditioned aversion or reduced palatability, leading to decreased reinforcing value of alcohol rather than specific anti-craving neuroadaptations.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Alcohol intake reductions persist when nausea is controlled for (e.g., antiemetic co-treatment or analyses adjusting for nausea severity) and when using GLP-1RA dosing regimens that minimize GI side effects, indicating effects beyond aversion.

plan.description: Locate trials reporting nausea/GI adverse events alongside alcohol outcomes; evaluate whether alcohol reductions track nausea severity and whether effects remain after adjustment.
resources_needed: Methods on controlling aversive side effects

args.task_description: Evaluate whether GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce alcohol use disorder symptoms, and map likely neurobiological mechanisms.

hypotheses.content: In adults with alcohol use disorder, GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment reduces heavy drinking days versus placebo/usual care over 12–24 weeks.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Falsified if one or more adequately powered randomized controlled trials (with preregistered outcomes and acceptable adherence/retention) show no clinically meaningful between-group reduction in heavy drinking days (e.g., effect size near zero with confidence intervals excluding a minimal clinically important difference) compared to placebo/usual care.

plan.description: Search RCTs and quasi-experimental studies of GLP-1 RAs in AUD or high-risk drinking; extract outcomes (heavy drinking days, total alcohol consumption, craving scales), adherence, and co-interventions; assess risk of bias and heterogeneity.

hypotheses.content: Any apparent reduction in alcohol intake during GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment is substantially mediated by weight loss/appetite suppression rather than a direct effect on alcohol reward circuitry.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Falsified if studies controlling for weight change (or using designs where weight change is minimal) still demonstrate robust reductions in alcohol intake/craving, or if mediation analyses show little-to-no mediation by weight/appetite changes.

plan.description: Identify trials reporting both alcohol outcomes and weight change; evaluate mediation/adjustment approaches; compare effects in weight-stable contexts (short-term dosing, matched-calorie controls where available).
resources_needed: individual trial reports with weight trajectories

hypotheses.content: GLP-1 receptor agonists improve AUD-related outcomes most in subgroups with comorbid obesity/insulin resistance, suggesting metabolic phenotype moderates treatment response.
hypotheses.falsification_criteria: Falsified if subgroup or interaction analyses across multiple studies show no differential effect by BMI/metabolic markers (and confidence intervals exclude clinically meaningful moderation), or if effects are equal/greater in lean/non–insulin-resistant participants.

plan.description: Compile evidence on effect modification by BMI, HbA1c, fasting insulin, or metabolic syndrome; prioritize preregistered subgroup analyses; rate credibility of subgroup findings.
